newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech transmitter shares rated "hold".
newsitem.headline: Czech transmitter shares rated "hold".

text.p: Shares in Czech radio transmission company Ceske Radiokomunikace a.s. are still rated as a long term hold despite last year's drop in profit and the absence of dividend payments, analysts said.
Equity analysts polled by Reuters said the company, which has a monopoly position on the radio transmission network market, has strong potential for development.
"Development perspectives of the firm are good, and the shareholder structure is apparently stabilised," said Karel Vojacek of Expandia Finance.
"Shares in this company should be a part of every quality portfolio," added Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka's Ivan Masar.
The firm's shares, which are traded on the main market of the Prague Stock Exchange, rose 18 crowns on Tuesday to 3,540, at which level analysts recommend holding the stock.
They suggested that the "buy" level was 3,500 crowns.
The company posted a preliminary 1996 gross profit of 161 million crowns, down 45 million from 1995, and analysts expect the figure will be revised further downward after the audit is completed.
"The company is going through an audit, there will be certain changes from the preliminary results," said Akro Capital's Michal Kusak.
"The gross profit should fall from (1995's) 206 milLion to 155 million," said Hana Kozusznikova of Brno Broker Group.

Respondents to the Reuters survey said that the fall in profits was mainly caused by the start-up of a mobile telephone network run by RadioMobil, a joint venture between Radiokomunikace and Germany's DeTeMobil in September 1996.

"The reason for lower profit are costs of some 100 million crowns connected with the launch of the digital mobile telephone network of RadioMobil, where Radiokomunikace have a 51 percent share," said Kozuzsnikova.
The firm plans to increase its gross profit to 181 million crowns this year on rising sales. Masar said he viewed the company's financial position as stable and healthy.

Radiokomunikace plans no dividend payouts until at least 2000 and reinvestment of all profits until that time. Investments should reach 880 million crowns this year, of which 500 million crowns should be raised by a bank loan or a share issue.
"If the increase in basic cpaital materialises, its form could significantly affect the share price," said Leos Jirman of Delta Securities.
He added that if the state privatisation agency, the National Property Fund, which holds 71 percent of the company, does not take part in the issue, increased free-float will help the shares.
Radiokomunikace is considered to be a strategic company, and any sell-off of the states holding must be approved by the government.
